summary: Social media users are comfortable signalling a quick reaction such as a thumbs up or smiley to a post. This experimental specification gives Internet Mail a similar facility, a way to indicate a summary reaction to a message.

plainLanguage.summary: On chat apps you can tap a thumbs up on a message. This experiment brings that to email, so a reply can be a quick reaction.

questions: how to send emoji reaction in email
subtitle: Bringing social media style reactions to email messages

tldr.problem: Social media users expect to quickly signal reactions like thumbs-up or emoji to messages, but email has no established way to send a reaction as a structured message rather than as reply text.
tldr.mechanism: A new Content-Disposition value of 'reaction' marks message parts as emoji reactions. Recipients' mail clients can parse the emoji, associate it with the original message via the In-Reply-To field, and display it separately from regular replies.
tldr.outcome: Mail clients can now display reactions distinctively, offering a familiar interaction model from social platforms. The document is Experimental to assess market interest and usability.

today: RFC 9078 is an Experimental specification published in August 2021. Adoption by mail clients has been limited, and the feature remains uncommon. The Experimental status allows further development based on real-world deployment experience.

sections.title: Reactions in Email
sections.content:
Social media and instant messaging platforms have trained users to signal quick reactions to posts—a thumbs-up, heart, smiley, or other emoji—without writing a full reply. This lightweight interaction is popular and efficient.

Email has long been able to include emoji in message bodies, but there has been no standard way to mark them as a reaction to an earlier message rather than as part of conversational content. This RFC defines that mechanism: a new Content-Disposition value called reaction lets a message part contain only emoji, semantically linked to the original message via the In-Reply-To header field.

By structuring reactions, mail clients can display them distinctly—perhaps as a count of reactions near the original message, similar to social media—rather than as a separate reply in the thread.
sections.plainLanguage: Email can carry emoji, but there was no way to say 'this emoji is a reaction to that message' instead of 'I am saying this in my reply'. This RFC adds a marker so mail apps can show reactions like social media does.

sections.title: The Reaction Mechanism
sections.content:
A reaction is a message part with Content-Disposition: reaction and Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8. The content is a single line of one or more emoji, separated by whitespace. The RFC defines a base set of five common reactions (thumbs-up, thumbs-down, grinning-face, frowning-face, crying-face) but does not restrict implementations to them—any valid Unicode emoji sequences are permitted.

A reaction message is sent as a reply, so it has an In-Reply-To field pointing to the original message's Message-ID. The mail client that receives it parses the emoji and, if they are valid according to Unicode Technical Standard 51, processes them as reactions to the cited message.

Because reactions are structured, a mail client can handle invalid emoji gracefully, treating candidates individually rather than rejecting the entire part. The RFC notes that emoji validation is non-trivial and advises implementers to use existing Unicode libraries rather than building validation from scratch.
sections.plainLanguage: A reaction message is a reply with a special marker saying 'reaction' and containing only emoji. The mail app looks at the In-Reply-To field to know which message the emoji is for.

sections.title: Processing and Display
sections.content:
When a mail client receives a message, it checks the In-Reply-To field to see if it references a message the client knows about. If it does, it looks for a message part with Content-Disposition: reaction. If found and valid, the client removes that part from the message view and processes it as a reaction.

How reactions are displayed is up to the mail client. One approach is a summary line showing emoji and a count (for example, '5 thumbs-up'). Another is to display reactions near the original message in a thread view. The RFC emphasizes that the handling is MUA-specific and leaves the user experience to implementers. Different mail clients may display the same reactions differently, just as they display threads differently today.
sections.plainLanguage: When a mail app sees a reaction message, it finds the message being replied to and shows the emoji next to it, not as a separate reply. How it looks is up to the app.

sections.title: Security and Usability
sections.content:
Reactions introduce no new content-specific security concerns because they are a constrained subset of existing email content: plain text with emoji. However, specialized processing of reactions could introduce vulnerabilities. Because reactions may spawn new user interaction features, there is potential for social engineering, as with any new user-facing capability.

The RFC highlights that emoji meaning is culturally context-dependent. A thumbs-up may have positive connotations in some cultures and negative in others. Mail clients must be aware that a sender's intent and a recipient's interpretation may differ. Designers should tread carefully when creating UI around reactions.
sections.plainLanguage: Reactions are just emoji, which email already has, so there is no new security risk from the emoji themselves. But how people use them can vary by culture, so apps need to be careful about how they display them.

sections.title: Experimental Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 9078 is Experimental. It was developed outside the IETF through private discussion and mailing list debate, with significant feedback shaping the final design. The Experimental status lets the community experiment with reactions in real implementations and gather data on adoption, usability, and any unforeseen issues.

The standard is designed to be straightforward to implement—it reuses existing MIME mechanisms—but the user experience design is paramount and left to mail client vendors. The experiment will inform whether a Standards Track version is warranted.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a test to see if mail programs will add reactions and if people will use them. If it works well and causes no problems, it can become a permanent email feature.
